extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent applicants, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed subject matter is adequately described in the originally filed application (35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph), and related rules on amendments, new matter, claim scope changes, ranges, genus/species issues, and examiner burden. Intended to direct examiner actions and inform applicants of support/new-matter risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of the claim need not be described literally (i.e., using the same terms or in haec verba) in order for the disclosure to satisfy the description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed, involving a departure from, addition to, or deletion from the disclosure of the application as filed, the examiner should conclude that the claimed subject matter is not described in that application. This conclusion will result in rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, or denial of benefit of a filing date as appropriate. See MPEP § 2163 for examination guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment affecting a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to the claims or the addition of a new claim must be supported by the description of the invention in the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An amendment to the specification (e.g., a change in the definition of a term used both in the specification and claim) may indirectly affect a claim even though no actual amendment is made to the claim. Examiner must ensure support exists in the original disclosure for any added or modified claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit of earlier U.S. filing date (35 U.S.C. 120)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of an earlier-filed U.S. application's filing date only if the subject matter of the claim is disclosed in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph) in the earlier-filed application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board/court evaluations may look for concrete disclosure (not mere 'laundry list' recitations) and for 'sufficient blaze marks' indicating the subset claimed. Lack of adequate blaze marks or only a compendium recitation can defeat entitlement to the earlier date (see cited cases like Tronzo v. Biomet and Regents of Univ. of Minnesota v. Gilead Scis., Inc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign priority / provisional benefit (35 U.S.C. 119)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of a foreign priority date or a provisional application filing date only if the corresponding earlier application supports the claims 'in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should verify that the earlier-filed foreign or provisional application contains the requisite disclosure to support the claimed subject matter (see cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for claim corresponding to an interference count
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim corresponding to a count in an interference must be supported by the specification in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking benefit of an earlier-filed U.S. application in an interference, the earlier application must meet 112(a) support for the subject matter of the count. Generic disclosures that do not specifically describe the claimed species may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claim adequacy (presumption and rebuttal)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description is present in the specification as filed, but an original claim may nonetheless lack written description support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical failures include (1) claims defined in functional language specifying a desired result without identifying how the function is performed, and (2) broad genus claims when the disclosure only describes a narrow species without evidence that the genus is contemplated. Mere appearance of claim language in ipsis verbis in the specification does not necessarily satisfy the requirement. Examiner should consult MPEP § 2163 subsections for rebutting the presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness of means-plus-function (112(f)) limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A means- (or step-) plus-function limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents; if the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure/materials/acts that perform the entire claimed function, the limitation is indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a limitation also lacks adequate written description because an indefinite, unbounded functional limitation would cover all ways of performing a function and indicate lack of possession. See 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA 6th paragraph), 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 2nd paragraph), and MPEP § 2181. Cite In re Donaldson Co., en banc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner burden in challenging written description
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry into whether the description requirement is met is a question of fact; the description as filed is presumed adequate unless and until the examiner rebuts that presumption with sufficient evidence or reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must have a reasonable basis to challenge adequacy and has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure a description of the claimed invention. The examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting a lack of written description conclusion (see MPEP § 2163).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of rejection requirements (what examiner must state)
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact which support the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These findings should (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at filing would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention given the application disclosure. General allegations (e.g., 'unpredictability in the art') are insufficient; a simple, pointed statement identifying the unsupported limitation may be sufficient in some circumstances. Suggest amendments when appropriate, but avoid adding new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to applicant's reply (when to repeat rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon applicant reply, before repeating any written-description rejection, review the basis for the rejection in view of the entire record, including amendments, arguments, and evidence submitted by applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record demonstrates the written description requirement is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection in the next Office action. If it still does not, repeat the rejection, fully respond to applicant's rebuttal arguments, and analyze any affidavits relevant to the written description issue. See In re Alton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes to scope of claims must be supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to meet the written description requirement commonly arises when claims are changed after filing to broaden or narrow breadth, alter a numerical range, or use terminology not synonymous with the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and to be entitled to earlier priority dates (35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 365(c)), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure. See MPEP § 2163 for examples and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening by omission of a limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation can raise whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; a claim that omits an element described as essential or critical in the specification does not comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification describes a feature as 'essential' or 'the only possible location', omitting it may render the broadened claim unsupported (see Gentry Gallery, Tronzo, In re Wilder). An omitted essential element can also cause enablement or indefiniteness rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claims and representative species (addition of generic claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description for a claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species; the 'representative number' must reflect the variation within the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where substantial variation exists within the genus, describe sufficient species to reflect that variation. Disclosure of only one species may suffice only if the disclosure indicates patentee invented species sufficient to constitute the genus. Courts have found both supporting and non-supporting outcomes depending on predictability and evidence (see AbbVie, Enzo Biochem, In re Curtis, In re Rasmussen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of claim changes that narrow claims by adding elements or limitations not supported by as-filed disclosure violates the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subgeneric terminology may or may not be acceptable—each case depends on what is reasonably communicated to those skilled in the art. Cite cases like Fujikawa, In re Ruschig, In re Lukach, Ex parte Sorenson. Examiner must evaluate facts to determine whether subgeneric language is described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical range limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: When changing numerical range limitations, analysis must consider which ranges one skilled in the art would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An example: original ranges of '25%-60%' and examples of '36%' and '50%' did not support a later claim to 'at least 35%' because 'at least' lacked an upper bound and covered embodiments outside disclosed range; however, 'between 35% and 60%' did meet the description requirement in that case. Courts differ by facts (see In re Wertheim, Purdue Pharma, General Hosp. Corp. v. Sienna).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of written description to new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding information to the abstract, specification, or drawings that is not described in the application as filed raises a 'new matter' issue; information from any one part of the originally filed application may be moved to any other part without introducing new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 132 and 251 prohibit introduction of new matter. If new subject matter is added to the disclosure, examiner should object under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 and require applicant to cancel the new matter. If new matter is added to the claims, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment when specification amended to add new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: When specification is amended to add new matter (even if claims are not amended), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) should be made whenever any claim limitations are affected by the added material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should still consider prior art rejections in view of the new matter since applicant may overcome new matter rejection. Applicant should specifically point out support for any amendments made to the disclosure, especially when filed in reply to an objection or rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review and appealability of new matter objections/rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily an objection is petitionable and a rejection is appealable; when the objection is 'determinative of the rejection' (e.g., examiner indicates disclosure contains new matter), the matter may be addressed by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims and specification or drawings contain new matter and there has been both a rejection and objection by the examiner, the issue becomes appealable and should not be decided by petition. See MPEP § 1201.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed subject matter disclosed only in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application as originally filed contains a claim disclosing material not disclosed in the remainder of the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure. Use Form paragraph 7.44 where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification. See In re Benno.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments supported in the original description are not new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to an application which are supported in the original description are NOT new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere rephrasing where the same meaning remains intact is permissible (In re Anderson). Inclusion of dictionary or art-recognized definitions known at time of filing may not be new matter. However, if multiple definitions exist and a particular definition is added, the application as filed must clearly indicate that the applicant intended that particular definition to avoid new matter or written description issues (see Schering Corp. v. Amgen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rephrasing permitted if meaning unchanged
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere rephrasing of a passage does not constitute new matter; a rewording is permissible where the same meaning remains intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere inclusion of dictionary or art-recognized definitions known at the time of filing may not be considered new matter. But adding a specific definition where multiple meanings exist requires that the original disclosure clearly indicate intent to use that definition to avoid new matter problems.
